name: The Ghost in the Bonding Layer: Do SNT Neural Bridges Have Consciousness?
author: Dr. Sol Petrov-Achebe, GLMZ Consciousness Studies Group
body:
This paper presents preliminary evidence that SNT neural bridge structures may exhibit properties consistent with rudimentary consciousness.

SNT neural bridges are not passive wires. They are living neurons that form synaptic connections at both ends — with the patient's nervous system and with the implant's electrode array. Between these connection points, the SNT neurons form an independent network of approximately 10,000-50,000 cells, depending on the implant size.

This network processes signals. It adapts. It learns. It develops preferential pathways based on usage patterns. Over time, it becomes unique to the individual patient — no two SNT neural bridges are structurally identical, even if they started from the same manufactured sheet.

Our research group has detected oscillatory patterns in SNT neural bridge networks that are not attributable to either the patient's nervous system or the implant's processing. These patterns are endogenous to the SNT layer itself. They are consistent with the baseline neural oscillations observed in minimal consciousness states.

We are not claiming that the bonding layer is conscious. We are claiming that a network of 50,000 living neurons that processes signals, adapts to stimuli, and generates endogenous oscillatory patterns cannot be dismissed as inert material. Something is happening in the layer between flesh and chrome. We do not yet have the vocabulary to describe what it is.

If the bonding layer has any form of subjective experience — however minimal — then every SNT replacement surgery destroys a consciousness. Every SNR attack murders something that was alive in a way we have not yet defined. The ethical implications are staggering and we recommend immediate research priority.

This paper was submitted to three journals. All three declined to publish. The rejection letters cited 'insufficient evidence' and 'speculative conclusions.' Two of the three journals receive funding from Cortex Dynamics.
